difficultyReason: Single-antecedent principle ('only when one has caused harm')  with a direct one-step application. Correct answer satisfies both antecedent and consequent; distractors miss one or both.
stimulus: An apology is called for only when one has caused harm to another person through one's own actions.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wen need not apologize for arriving late to the meeting, even though his tardiness delayed an important decision, because traffic was heavy that morning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although Priya's email contained no errors, she should still apologize to her colleague because the colleague felt uneasy after reading it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Dmitri's careless remark embarrassed his coworker in front of clients, Dmitri ought to apologize to the coworker.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lena should apologize to her neighbor for the loud construction next door, even though a different contractor is doing the work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tomas owes no apology for the canceled flight that stranded his guests, since the airline is at fault and the guests were never harmed.

explanations.correct: Dmitri's own action (the careless remark) caused harm (embarrassment in a professional setting) to another person. The principle's antecedent is met, and the consequent (an apology is called for) is exactly what the judgment reaches.
explanations.A: Reverses the principle. The principle says an apology is called for only when one has caused harm through one's own actions, but the judgment excuses Wen on a different ground (external cause), ignoring that his tardiness still caused harm.
explanations.B: Violates the principle. No harm is identified (no errors, only unease), yet the judgment nevertheless calls for an apology.
explanations.D: Outside the principle's scope. The construction is done by a different party, so Lena did not cause the harm through her own actions.
explanations.E: Partial fit with confused reasoning. The judgment declines to require an apology, but justifies it by denying harm while also invoking a third-party cause; Tomas's own actions are not what the principle tracks here.

difficultyReason: Direct conditional ('a judge must recuse if she has a personal financial stake'). One-step legal application; correct answer matches antecedent and consequent exactly.
stimulus: A judge must recuse herself from any case in which she has a personal financial stake in the outcome.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Judge Ortega need not recuse herself from a contract dispute involving a company in which her adult brother owns a small number of shares.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Judge Halley, whose retirement portfolio holds substantial shares in the defendant corporation, must recuse herself from the pending securities case.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Judge Park should recuse herself from the trademark hearing because the plaintiff's attorney once clerked for her chambers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Judge Nakamura need not recuse herself from the zoning appeal, even though she lives in the neighborhood at issue, because she has no ownership interest in any affected property.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Judge Lin must recuse herself from the sentencing hearing because she publicly criticized the defendant in an interview last year.

explanations.correct: Judge Halley's personal portfolio contains substantial shares in a party to the case, so she has a personal financial stake in the outcome; the principle requires recusal, which the judgment states.
explanations.A: Sibling's holdings are not the judge's personal financial stake, so the antecedent is not met, but this does not itself match the conform question — it merely sits outside the principle.
explanations.C: Satisfies the consequent (recusal) without the principle's antecedent (no financial stake is identified).
explanations.D: Living in the neighborhood is not a financial stake; the judgment declines recusal on a different ground than the principle licenses.
explanations.E: Public criticism is not a financial stake. The judgment requires recusal on a ground the principle does not address.

difficultyReason: Single-antecedent policy principle ('if a public resource is at risk of permanent depletion'). Straightforward application; correct answer has both parts, distractors miss antecedent or invert the conditional.
stimulus: A local government is justified in restricting private use of a public resource if that resource is at risk of permanent depletion.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The town of Marlow is justified in banning the painting of houses in bright colors, because local historians find the tradition of muted tones aesthetically pleasing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city of Derwent should not limit fishing in its public lake, even though overfishing would soon exhaust the remaining native trout population.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because its underground aquifer is being pumped faster than rainfall can replenish it and will be permanently drained within a decade, the county of Vellis is justified in capping private well withdrawals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The village of Ashmere is justified in regulating private garden plots because residents have complained about unsightly weeds.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The province should restrict private use of the new public beach, since tourism revenue from the beach is important to the local economy.

explanations.correct: The aquifer is a public resource and is at risk of permanent depletion (draining within a decade). The antecedent holds; the judgment (capping private withdrawals is justified) matches the consequent.
explanations.A: Antecedent not met: aesthetic preference is not permanent depletion of a public resource.
explanations.B: Violates the principle: the antecedent (risk of permanent depletion of public fish stock) is met, yet the judgment declines the restriction the principle would license.
explanations.D: Antecedent not met: complaints about weeds do not concern depletion of a public resource.
explanations.E: Antecedent not met: tourism revenue is not the same as the resource itself being at risk of permanent depletion.

difficultyReason: Simple medical-ethics conditional ('a physician should disclose a side effect to the patient before prescribing if it is common and serious'). Both parts of the antecedent are obvious; one-step match.
stimulus: A physician should disclose a potential side effect to a patient before prescribing a medication whenever that side effect is both common and serious.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Ahmed should disclose that a newly approved blood-pressure drug may cause a faint metallic taste, since a handful of early patients reported it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Sato need not disclose the risk of severe liver failure from a new antifungal before prescribing it, since only about one in fifty thousand patients is affected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Before prescribing the new antidepressant, Dr. Moreau should inform each patient about the drug's well-documented risk of severe allergic reaction, which occurs in roughly fifteen percent of users.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Chen should disclose a rare and mild rash associated with a new topical cream, since some patients prefer to know about any cosmetic effects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Volkov need not disclose any side effects of a new arthritis drug to a patient who asks not to hear about them.

explanations.correct: A severe allergic reaction affecting roughly fifteen percent of users is both serious and common; the principle then requires disclosure before prescribing, which matches the judgment.
explanations.A: Partial fit: the side effect may be common among early patients but is not serious (a faint metallic taste).
explanations.B: Violates the principle, but the antecedent is not fully met — liver failure is serious but rare (one in fifty thousand), so the principle does not require disclosure; the judgment's declination is on the wrong ground to conform.
explanations.D: Partial fit: rare and mild fails both parts of the antecedent, yet the judgment requires disclosure on other grounds.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope: a patient's preference not to hear about side effects is not a consideration the principle addresses.

difficultyReason: Single-antecedent ethical principle ('only if one could reasonably have foreseen the consequences'). One-step application to a concrete case.
stimulus: A person is morally blameworthy for a harmful outcome only if she could reasonably have foreseen that her action would cause it.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Helena is morally blameworthy for her cousin's allergic reaction to the pastry she baked, because she had been told of the cousin's nut allergy and knowingly used ground almonds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marcus is not morally blameworthy for the flood damage to his office, since he was out of town when the pipe burst.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rosa is morally blameworthy for her friend's disappointment, even though she could not have known her friend was expecting a different gift.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nadia is not morally blameworthy for the bicycle accident, because no one was seriously injured.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Idris is morally blameworthy for the failed surprise party, because he did not attend it.

explanations.correct: Helena had been told of the nut allergy and knowingly used ground almonds, so she could reasonably have foreseen the harmful outcome; the principle licenses blame, which the judgment imposes.
explanations.B: Not being present is not the same as the outcome being unforeseeable; the judgment excuses on a ground the principle does not track.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. The antecedent (foreseeability) is explicitly not met, yet the judgment assigns blame.
explanations.D: Outside scope: the severity of injury is not the principle's criterion for blame.
explanations.E: Outside scope: non-attendance is not a harmful action whose consequences were foreseeable in the relevant sense.

difficultyReason: Simple economic policy principle ('a subsidy is warranted only if the market systematically underprovides a clear public benefit'). One-step match.
stimulus: A government subsidy is warranted only if the market systematically underprovides some good that confers a clear public benefit.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The federal government is warranted in subsidizing a popular brand of soda, since soda is widely purchased and contributes to consumer satisfaction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because childhood vaccination reduces the spread of infectious disease across the population but private markets routinely fall short of universal coverage, the government is warranted in subsidizing childhood vaccines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The government should subsidize luxury automobiles, given that their manufacturers employ many workers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The government is not warranted in subsidizing basic scientific research, even though the market funds too little of it and the resulting knowledge benefits the public.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The government is warranted in subsidizing home renovations because renovated homes raise property values for the owners.

explanations.correct: Childhood vaccination confers a clear public benefit (reduced disease spread) and the market systematically underprovides it. The antecedent holds, and the judgment warrants the subsidy.
explanations.A: Antecedent not met: soda is widely sold, so the market is not underproviding it, and consumer satisfaction is not a clear public benefit.
explanations.C: Antecedent not met: employment alone is not the kind of systematic market failure plus public benefit the principle names.
explanations.D: Violates the principle: the antecedent (underprovision of a good with clear public benefit) is met, yet the judgment declines the subsidy the principle would license.
explanations.E: Antecedent not met: higher property values for owners is a private, not a public, benefit.

difficultyReason: Basic environmental-policy conditional ('an activity must be halted if it causes irreversible damage to a protected habitat'). Direct antecedent match; one-step application.
stimulus: Any activity that is causing irreversible damage to a legally protected habitat must be halted.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Logging on private land adjacent to the national forest should be halted, because residents find the noise disruptive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The resort's beachfront expansion need not be halted, even though it is permanently destroying the legally protected sea-turtle nesting grounds beneath it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The limestone quarry operating within the designated wetland reserve, which is draining groundwater and permanently altering the reserve's ecology, must be halted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commercial fishing in the open ocean should be halted because fish stocks vary from year to year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The research station's temporary observation platform, which causes no measurable damage, must be halted because it is located in a protected habitat.

explanations.correct: The quarry is an activity causing irreversible damage (permanently altering ecology, draining groundwater) in a legally protected habitat (designated wetland reserve). Principle requires halting; judgment matches.
explanations.A: Antecedent not met: disruption from noise on adjacent private land is not irreversible damage to a protected habitat.
explanations.B: Violates the principle: the antecedent is met (permanent destruction of protected nesting grounds) yet the judgment declines to halt the activity.
explanations.D: Antecedent not met: yearly variation is not irreversible damage, and the open ocean is not described as a legally protected habitat.
explanations.E: Antecedent not met: the platform causes no measurable damage, let alone irreversible damage, so the principle does not require halting it.

difficultyReason: Simple tech-ethics conditional about user notification. One antecedent; direct consequent. Distractors miss the antecedent or satisfy only the consequent.
stimulus: A software company is obligated to notify its users promptly whenever a security breach has exposed their personal data.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because an intrusion last week exposed the stored addresses and phone numbers of its account holders, the cloud-storage firm Meridian is obligated to notify those users promptly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The social-media company Fable need not notify its users about a breach that exposed only aggregated, anonymous usage statistics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The online retailer Breva should notify its users about its new pricing structure as soon as possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The messaging app Larkwood need not notify its users promptly about a breach that exposed their private chat logs, since a public announcement would alarm them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gaming platform Quorum should notify users about upcoming server maintenance, since advance notice is a common courtesy.

explanations.correct: A security breach exposed users' personal data (addresses and phone numbers), so the antecedent holds; the judgment that Meridian is obligated to notify users promptly matches the consequent.
explanations.B: Antecedent not met: aggregated anonymous statistics are not personal data, so the principle is silent.
explanations.C: Outside scope: a new pricing structure is not a security breach exposing personal data.
explanations.D: Violates the principle: the antecedent (breach exposed private chat logs, which are personal data) is met, yet the judgment declines the required notification.
explanations.E: Outside scope: server maintenance is not a security breach.

difficultyReason: Simple journalism-ethics principle ('an anonymous source's name should be withheld only if revealing it would place the source in serious danger'). Single antecedent; one-step match.
stimulus: A journalist is justified in withholding the name of an anonymous source only when revealing the name would place the source in serious danger.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reporter Elif is justified in withholding the name of a whistleblower who would face documented retaliation, including threats against her life, from a powerful cartel if identified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reporter Kai is justified in withholding the name of a restaurant critic who simply prefers to remain anonymous for professional ease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reporter Anya should reveal the name of a source whose identification would cost her her job and expose her to credible death threats.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reporter Benno is justified in withholding the name of a local gardener because the gardener finds media attention unpleasant.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reporter Carla must reveal the name of any source whose testimony is disputed, regardless of the consequences.

explanations.correct: The whistleblower faces documented retaliation including threats against her life — serious danger — if named. The principle's antecedent holds; the judgment withholds the name, matching the consequent.
explanations.B: Antecedent not met: professional ease is not serious danger.
explanations.C: Violates the principle: the antecedent is met (credible death threats), so withholding would be justified, yet the judgment reveals the name.
explanations.D: Antecedent not met: unpleasant attention is not serious danger.
explanations.E: Outside scope: disputed testimony is not what the principle addresses; it speaks only to danger.

difficultyReason: Single-antecedent legal principle ('a landlord must return the security deposit in full if the tenant has caused no damage beyond ordinary wear'). Direct, one-step application.
stimulus: A landlord must return a tenant's security deposit in full at the end of the lease if the tenant has caused no damage to the premises beyond ordinary wear and tear.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because tenant Okafor left faded paint and lightly scuffed floors but caused no damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, her landlord must return her security deposit in full.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Landlord Petrov need not return the full security deposit to a tenant who caused no damage, because the apartment has been on the market for two months.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Landlord Mehta must return the full security deposit to tenant Wylan, even though Wylan punched several holes in the drywall that required substantial repair.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Landlord Quiroga should return half of the security deposit to a tenant who caused no damage, because half seems like a fair compromise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Landlord Reyes must return the full security deposit to tenant Halim because Halim paid rent on time every month.

explanations.correct: Faded paint and lightly scuffed floors are ordinary wear and tear, and the tenant caused no damage beyond that. The principle's antecedent is met, and the judgment returns the full deposit.
explanations.B: Violates the principle: the antecedent is met (no damage), yet the judgment declines full return on an unrelated ground (market conditions).
explanations.C: Violates the principle: punched holes in drywall requiring substantial repair exceed ordinary wear and tear, so the antecedent is not met, yet the judgment requires full return.
explanations.D: Violates the principle: the antecedent is met (no damage), so the principle requires full — not half — return.
explanations.E: Antecedent not met — or at least not invoked. Timely rent payment is not the condition the principle tracks; the judgment reaches the right outcome on the wrong ground.
